lessons.title: Of Studies — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Of Studies is a famous essay by Francis Bacon (1561–1626), the English philosopher and statesman who laid the groundwork of the modern scientific method. Bacon explains what studies are for, how different books should be read, and how the right study can cure defects of the mind.

Three Uses of Studies

  • Studies serve for delight — their chief use for delight is in privateness and retiring (when a man is alone).
  • Studies serve for ornament — they grace our discourse and conversation.
  • Studies serve for ability — they help in the judgment and disposition (handling) of business; general counsels and the marshalling of affairs come best from learned men.

The Right Balance

Bacon warns against misuse: to spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament is affectation; and to make judgment wholly by their rules is the humour of a scholar. Studies perfect nature, and are perfected by experience — natural abilities are like natural plants that need pruning by study, while studies give directions too large unless they are bounded in by experience. Crafty men condemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them. We should read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted, nor to find talk and discourse, but to weigh and consider.

How Books Should Be Read

  • Some books are to be tasted — read only in parts.
  • Others are to be swallowed — read fully, but not curiously (not with deep attention).
  • Some few are to be chewed and digested — read wholly, with diligence and attention.
  • Some books may be read by deputy (through extracts made by others), but only the less important ones; distilled books are like common distilled waters — flashy things.

Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. So a man who writes little needs a great memory; a man who confers little needs a present wit; and a man who reads little needs much cunning, to seem to know what he does not.

What Each Study Gives

  • Histories make men wise.
  • Poets make men witty.
  • Mathematics makes men subtle.
  • Natural philosophy makes men deep.
  • Moral philosophy makes men grave.
  • Logic and rhetoric make men able to contend (argue).

Bacon's motto is "Abeunt studia in mores" — studies pass into and influence manners.

Studies Cure Defects of the Mind

Just as diseases of the body have appropriate exercises — bowling for the stone and reins, shooting for the lungs and breast, gentle walking for the stomach, riding for the head — every defect of the mind may have a special receipt (remedy). If a man's wit is wandering, let him study mathematics, for in demonstrations he must begin again if his mind is called away. If his wit is not apt to distinguish differences, let him study the schoolmen, who are cymini sectores (splitters of hair). If he is not apt to beat over matters and call up one thing to prove another, let him study the lawyers' cases.

Key Points

  • Studies serve for delight, ornament and ability.
  • Too much study is sloth; too much show is affectation; judging only by book rules is the humour of a scholar.
  • Books are to be tasted, swallowed, or chewed and digested, according to their worth.
  • Reading makes a full man, conference a ready man, and writing an exact man.
  • Every defect of the mind has a special study as its remedy.

The book's Glossary explains the difficult words of Bacon's essay. Learn these words with their meanings and their use in the essay.

Words and Meanings

Key Points

  • Ornament = decoration; disposition = arrangement or mind-set.
  • Confute means to disprove; a receipt is a remedy.
  • Cymini sectores are hairsplitters — men who split very fine differences.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 1 teaches figurative language and nuances of meaning, and the four kinds of sentences.

Figurative Language and Nuances

Nuance means the shades of meaning created by subtle differences in word meaning and usage. The book's example is house and home: both words denote a place where one lives (their denotation), but "home" carries emotional connotations of warmth, security and childhood that "house" may lack.

  • Figurative use: "The pen is mightier than the sword" — pen means writing and ideas, sword means weapons and war.
  • Literal use: "She is writing with a blue pen" — pen is used in its ordinary, physical sense.
  • Figurative use: "He is an institute in himself" — the man himself embodies knowledge and learning.
  • Literal use: "The institute will be closed tomorrow" — an actual building/organization.

The Sentence and Its Four Kinds

A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense. It begins with a capital letter, ends with a full stop (or question/exclamation mark), and always contains a finite verb. The four kinds are:

  • Declarative (Assertive) — gives information and ends with a full stop: I like fantasy novels. There is a white house around the corner.
  • Imperative — expresses a command, order or request: Close the door. Please pick up the notes when you come.
  • Interrogative — asks a question and ends with a question mark: What is the name of the movie you were watching? Can I come with you to the book fair?
  • Exclamatory — expresses sudden, strong emotion and ends with an exclamation mark: Wow, how good this is! That was a great match!

Finding Word Meanings (Word Detective Skills)

The unit also trains three strategies for unknown words: use context clues (guess from the sentence around the word), study word patterns (prefixes, suffixes and related forms, e.g. analyze – analysis – analytical), and verify with reference tools (dictionary, glossary, thesaurus) — then check the inferred meaning in a dictionary.

Key Points

  • Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling a word carries.
  • A sentence makes complete sense and contains a finite verb.
  • The four kinds of sentences are declarative, imperative, interrogative and exclamatory.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Are Doctors Men of Science? (George Bernard Shaw)

lessons.title: Are Doctors Men of Science? — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This essay is taken from the preface to George Bernard Shaw's play The Doctor's Dilemma (1906). With sharp satire, Shaw attacks the popular delusion that every doctor is a man of science.

Shaw's Main Charge

Shaw says the rank and file of doctors are no more scientific than their tailors. To a sufficiently ignorant man, every captain of a trading schooner looks like a Galileo and every piano-tuner like a Helmholtz — in the same way, ordinary people mistake a doctor's title for science. In truth, doctoring is an art, not a science: it is not even the art of keeping people in health, but only the art of curing illness. A layman who reads scientific journals may know more about science than most doctors, who practise only to earn their bread.

Why Doctors Are Not Scientific

  • A doctor rarely contributes to science; much oftener he draws disastrous conclusions from his clinical experience because he has no conception of scientific method and handles evidence and statistics without expertness.
  • The only real distinction between a quack and a qualified doctor is that the qualified one is authorized to sign death certificates — for which both seem to have about equal occasion.
  • Unqualified healers — bone-setters and herbalists — make fortunes from educated and wealthy patients, and some registered doctors themselves use heretical methods, having qualified only for convenience.

The Herbalist and the Doctor

The humblest healers are the herbalists, who wander the fields on Sundays seeking herbs like Virginia Snake Root, and on weekdays sell packets of pennyroyal and dandelion labelled with the diseases they are supposed to cure. Shaw says he can perceive no distinction between the science of the herbalist and that of the duly registered doctor. His example: a relative consulted a doctor for symptoms that merely indicated the need for a holiday; the doctor found her heart "a little depressed" and promptly gave a stiff dose of digitalis, the profession's labelled heart drug. The hardy old lady survived — and was converted to Christian Science. A farm labourer consulting a herbalist would have been treated in exactly the same way.

The Theme

The essay explores the duality of medicine as both a science and an art. It criticizes the idea that doctors rely only on scientific knowledge: their practice also involves habit, intuition and human judgment, and it raises ethical questions when a patient's interest conflicts with the doctor's personal gain. Shaw's two central ideas build on each other: once science is replaced by custom and tradition, profit and fashion enter freely — so medicine must return to evidence and service to earn the name of science.

Key Points

  • Shaw's charge: doctoring is an art, not a science; most doctors follow habit, not scientific method.
  • The qualified doctor differs from the quack mainly in being allowed to sign death certificates.
  • Shaw finds no difference between the herbalist's "science" and the registered doctor's.
  • The essay is satire: it makes the reader laugh while exposing a serious fault.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the hard words and the famous names Shaw mentions in the essay.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning

dupeA victim of deception; to deceive, to make a fool of someone.
hereticalUnorthodox — against accepted beliefs or practice.
disastrousCausing great or sudden misfortune.

Virginia snake rootAn American plant, believed by herbalists to cure disease.

trading schoonerA trading ship with two or more masts.

The Great Names in the Essay

  • Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) — Italian astronomer who proved that the earth and other planets move round the sun.
  • Beethoven (1770–1827) — the great German composer who crowned the classical age of music.
  • Helmholtz (1821–1894) — German physiologist and physicist, one of the greatest scientists of his age.
  • Solon (early 6th century BC) — Athenian statesman and poet, one of the Seven Sages, who laid the foundation of democracy.
  • Charles Darwin (1809–1882) — English naturalist famous for the theory of evolution in The Origin of Species.
  • George Stephenson (1781–1848) — English engineer, regarded as the father of railways.
  • Old Bailey — the central criminal court of London.

Shaw's point: just as every schooner captain is not a Galileo, every doctor is not a man of science.

Key Points

  • A quack is an unqualified doctor; a dupe is a person who is fooled.
  • Digitalis is a heart drug made from foxglove leaves.
  • Galileo, Darwin and Stephenson are Shaw's examples of real men of science.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 2 teaches how to consult reference materials, silent letters, punctuation marks, and transitional devices.

Using a Dictionary and a Thesaurus

  • A dictionary gives a word's meaning, pronunciation, spelling, part of speech, example sentences and etymology (word origin). If a word has several meanings, match the one that fits your context.
  • A thesaurus lists synonyms (words of similar meaning) and antonyms (opposites). Example: dilemma = a situation where a choice must be made between two difficult options; its synonyms are predicament, problem, puzzle.
  • Not all synonyms mean exactly the same thing — check a new synonym in the dictionary before using it.
  • Remember: the plural of analysis is analyses; in "She runs quickly", quickly is an adverb.

Silent Letters

A silent letter is written but not pronounced. Many English words have silent letters because of their Greek, Latin or French history.

WordSilent LetterPronunciation
knightk/nait/
honesth/on-ist/
psychologyp/sy-kol-o-jee/
wristw/rist/
islands/eye-land/
debtb/det/
subtleb/sut-l/
wouldl/wood/
knifek/naif/
doubtb/dout/
combb/koum/

Punctuation Marks

  • Full stop (.) ends a complete sentence: I like reading plays by George Bernard Shaw.
  • Comma (,) separates ideas, items in a list, or clauses: Shaw was a playwright, critic, and political thinker.
  • Question mark (?) ends a direct question: Are doctors really men of science?
  • Exclamation mark (!) shows strong feeling: What a brilliant argument Shaw made!
  • Apostrophe (') shows possession (Shaw's plays) or contraction (It's = It is).
  • Quotation marks (" ") show direct speech or a quotation.
  • Colon (:) introduces a list, an explanation or a quote: He bought three things: a book, a pen, and a dictionary.
  • Semicolon (;) joins two related sentences without a conjunction: Shaw was a great writer; his wit was unmatched.

Transitional Devices

Transitional devices (transition words) connect ideas, sentences and paragraphs and signal the relationship between them. The main groups are: Addition (moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides), Contrast (however, nevertheless, on the other hand, in contrast), Result (therefore, as a result, consequently, thus), Illustration (for example, for instance, such as), Comparison (similarly, likewise, just as), Order (first, secondly, finally, subsequently), Condition (if, unless, in case), Concession (although, even so, in spite of), Summary (in short, in conclusion, to sum up) and Generalisation (as a rule, in general, on the whole).

Key Points

  • A dictionary gives meaning and pronunciation; a thesaurus gives synonyms and antonyms.
  • Silent letters are written but not pronounced, e.g. k in knight, b in debt.
  • Punctuation makes writing clear, prevents miscommunication and adds tone and rhythm.
  • Transitional devices link ideas and show how they are related.

chapters.title: Unit 3: A Poison Tree (Poem - William Blake)

lessons.title: A Poison Tree — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
A Poison Tree is a famous poem by William Blake (1757–1827), the English poet, painter and printmaker of the Romantic Age. In only four short stanzas, Blake shows what happens when anger is spoken out — and what happens when it is hidden and nursed in secret.

Stanza 1: Two Kinds of Anger

The speaker was angry with his friend: he told his wrath, and his wrath did end. He was angry with his foe (enemy): he told it not, and his wrath did grow. Spoken anger disappears; hidden anger grows.

Stanza 2: The Anger Is Watered and Sunned

The speaker nurses his anger like a plant. He watered it in fears, night and morning with his tears, and he sunned it with smiles and with soft deceitful wiles (clever tricks used to deceive). Outwardly he smiles at his enemy; inwardly his hatred is fed every day.

Stanza 3: The Bright Apple

The anger-tree grew both day and night until it bore an apple bright. The foe beheld it shine and knew that it was the speaker's. The apple is the outward beauty of a hidden grudge — revenge or temptation dressed up to look attractive.

Stanza 4: The Foe Beneath the Tree

The foe stole into the speaker's garden when the night had veiled the pole (covered the sky). In the morning the speaker is glad to see his foe outstretched beneath the tree — dead, poisoned by the fruit of hidden hatred. The "gladness" is grim, not a victory: the poison has destroyed the enemy, and with him the speaker's own humanity.

Theme and Moral

The theme is the destructive power of suppressed anger and hatred. The poison tree is an extended metaphor for wrath that is never expressed: it is watered by fears and tears, sunned by false smiles, and finally bears deadly fruit. Blake's warning is a cautionary tale for all relationships: acknowledge and address your emotions honestly, because anger that is harboured in secret grows until it destroys. Communication ends anger; silence feeds it.

Key Points

  • Anger told to a friend ends; anger hidden from a foe grows.
  • The tree, its watering and sunning, and the bright apple are all symbols of a secret grudge.
  • The foe eats the poisoned fruit and is found dead beneath the tree.
  • Moral: unexpressed anger can grow into something destructive.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the words of the poem. Learn them with the lines where they appear.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
foeAn enemy or opponent. "I was angry with my foe."
wrathGreat anger. "I told my wrath, my wrath did end."
fearsFeelings of anxiety or dread. The speaker watered his wrath in fears.
sunnedExposed to sunlight. He sunned his anger with smiles, as a plant is sunned to grow.
deceitfulDishonest, intended to mislead.

gladFeeling pleasure or joy.
boreProduced or yielded. The tree bore an apple bright.

Note also night in the poem: literally the period of darkness, but symbolically it stands for danger and secrecy — the hidden growth of hatred.

Key Points

  • A foe is an enemy; wrath is great anger.
  • Wiles are clever tricks used to deceive.
  • Veiled means covered; outstretched means spread out fully.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 3 teaches the figures of speech — the devices by which words go beyond their literal meanings — and the intonation patterns of spoken English.

Figures of Speech

  • Simile — a comparison of two dissimilar things using "like" or "as": strong as an ox; sweet as sugar; raining like cats and dogs.
  • Metaphor — a direct comparison without "like" or "as"; it says one thing IS another: Time is money. Laughter is the best medicine. The whole poem "A Poison Tree" is an extended metaphor: anger is a tree.
  • Personification — giving human attributes to a thing, idea or animal: The sky weeps. The wind is whispering outside.
  • Apostrophe — addressing an absent person or a non-human thing as if it could reply: O death! Where is thy sting?
  • Alliteration — repetition of the same beginning consonant sound: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. She sells seashells on the seashore.
  • Anaphora — repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses: "I have a dream…" in Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech; "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…" in Dickens.
  • Refrain — a line or phrase repeated in a poem or song, e.g. "Tyger Tyger, burning bright" in Blake's "The Tyger".
  • Symbolism — a concrete image standing for an abstract idea: the heart symbolizes love, the dove peace, black death, an olive branch a truce. In the poem, the apple symbolizes revenge or temptation.
  • Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration for effect, not to be taken literally: I've told you a million times. She wept oceans of tears.
  • Imagery — descriptive language that appeals to the senses so the reader can see, hear, taste, touch and feel: His words felt like a dagger in my heart.
  • Irony — a situation that subverts (upsets) the reader's expectations, e.g. saying "Oh great" in response to bad news.
  • Antithesis — opposite ideas placed side by side for contrast: Speech is silver, but silence is golden. Man proposes, God disposes.
  • Onomatopoeia — a word whose sound suggests its meaning: buzz, boom, meow.

Intonation Patterns

Intonation is the melodic pattern of an utterance, involving stress and rhythm. English has three main patterns: falling intonation, rising intonation and fall-rise intonation. Reading the poem aloud with the right intonation brings out its feelings.

Key Points

  • A simile compares with "like/as"; a metaphor compares directly.
  • Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
  • Symbolism uses a concrete image for an abstract idea — the apple for revenge.
  • Intonation has three main patterns: falling, rising and fall-rise.

lessons.title: A New Microbe — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
A New Microbe is a humorous short story by O. Henry (1862–1910), the pen name of William Sydney Porter, whose stories of ordinary city people are famous for their gripping openings and the twist at the end.

The Amateur Scientist

A man of Houston, John, is a great lover of science and an ardent student of its mysteries. He has fitted up a small laboratory at home and spends much time experimenting with chemicals. Of late he has been deeply interested in germ theories: he has somewhat neglected his business to read Pasteur's and Koch's writings and everything he could procure about different kinds of bacilli, and he has bought a 900-power magnifying instrument, hoping to add his own discovery to the knowledge of germ life.

The Quiet Evening

On Tuesday night there was a sociable and supper at a church. His wife Ellen wanted him to go, but he begged off: he would rather stay home with his microscope while she took the children. He had been reading ex-Geologist Dumble's report on his analysis of Houston bayou water, and he was anxious to verify the statements by an examination of his own. After supper he found a tin bucket full of water by the hydrant in the kitchen, carried it to his laboratory, fastened himself in, and worked for nearly three hours, examining samples through the powerful microscope.

The "Discovery"

At last he slapped his hand on his knee in triumph: "Dumble is wrong!" The inhabitants of the water, he declared, were neither what Dumble had named them nor any known germ. "Can it be that I have discovered a new germ? Is scientific fame within my grasp?" He seized his pen and began to write. When his family returned, he welcomed his wife enthusiastically: since she had been gone, he had won fame and perhaps a fortune — a new bacterium in the bayou water, described nowhere in science. He would call it after her: "Ellenobes, or Ellenites, or what?" Ellen looked through the microscope at the "funny little round things" and asked if they were injurious. "Sure death," he said. "Get one of 'em in your alimentary canal, and you're a goner."

The Twist

Then Ellen caught sight of the bucket on the table and shrieked: "Oh, John, you smart one! You've got my bucket of Galveston oysters that I bought to take to the supper! Microbes, indeed!" The "new germ" was no germ at all — the great discovery was a bucket of oysters in their water. The story satirizes vanity and pretension: the amateur's pride in his "science" collapses in one line, and the reader laughs at how self-deception can spread like a microbe.

Elements of the Story

  • Characters: John, the protagonist (main character), and his wife Ellen.
  • Setting: John's small home laboratory in Houston, on a Tuesday evening.
  • Conflict: internal — John's vanity and self-deception against the plain facts.
  • Climax and resolution: Ellen's shriek exposes the bucket of oysters; the "discovery" ends in laughter.
  • Theme: vanity, pretension and the absurdity of human folly, shown through wit and irony.

Key Points

  • John, an amateur scientist, examines bucket water for three hours and "discovers" a new germ.
  • He plans to name the germ after his wife Ellen and win fame and fortune.
  • The twist: the bucket held Galveston oysters, not bayou water.
  • O. Henry's stories end with a characteristic twist of plot.

lessons.title: Unit 4 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the scientific words of the story.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
ardentShowing strong enthusiasm or intense emotion. John is an ardent student of science.
mysteriesThings that are difficult or impossible to understand or explain; secrets or unknown matters.
procureTo obtain something, especially with effort or care. He read everything he could procure about bacilli.

bacilliPlural of bacillus: rod-shaped bacteria, often harmful and capable of causing disease.

Who Is Called What?

The unit's exercise asks for the names of persons. A geology is the scientific study of the earth, and a geologist studies the origin and history of the rocks and soil of which the earth is made. In the same way:

  • A person who travels for pleasure — a tourist.
  • A person who studies science — a scientist.
  • An exceptionally intelligent person — a genius.
  • A person who bakes — a baker.
  • A person who keeps babies or takes care of babies — a babysitter (or nurse).
  • A person who is skilled in money matters — a financier.

Key Points

  • Ardent means full of enthusiasm; to procure is to obtain with effort.
  • Bacilli are rod-shaped bacteria; a bayou is a slow, marshy stream.
  • A geologist studies the earth; a tourist travels for pleasure.

lessons.title: Unit 4 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 4 teaches the eight parts of speech and the difference between idioms and proverbs.

The Eight Parts of Speech

The parts of speech explain how a word is used in a sentence. There are eight:

Part of SpeechFunctionExample
NounRepresents a person, place, thing, idea or animalThe dog barks.
VerbExpresses an action, state, or occurrenceShe runs quickly.
AdjectiveDescribes or modifies a noun or pronounHe is happy.
AdverbModifies a verb, adjective or another adverb; answers how, when, whereShe runs quickly.
PronounReplaces a noun or noun phraseHe is happy.
PrepositionShows the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and other wordsThe book is in the bag.
ConjunctionConnects words, phrases, or clausesShe reads and writes.
InterjectionExpresses some sudden feeling or emotionWow! That's amazing.

Skill in parts of speech grows in degrees of complexity: from simple sentences ("She runs fast") to complex ones ("Although she was tired, she ran swiftly to catch the bus"), in both speaking and writing.

Idioms and Proverbs

  • An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is figurative and different from the literal meanings of its words. Idioms are phrases, not complete sentences, and carry no moral: "Break a leg!" literally sounds like wishing a fracture; it actually means "Good luck!" (said to performers). "Break the ice" means to take a start or initiative.
  • A proverb is a short, well-known saying that contains advice or a general truth. Proverbs are complete sentences and can usually be understood even when heard for the first time: "Actions speak louder than words" — what you do is more important and believable than what you say.

Proverbs from the unit: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step; A picture is worth a thousand words; Beggars can't be choosers; Don't bite the hand that feeds you; The early bird catches the worm; A stitch in time saves nine; Honesty is the best policy; Rome wasn't built in a day.

Key Points

  • There are eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
  • An idiom's meaning is figurative; a proverb gives advice in a complete sentence.
  • "Break a leg" means good luck; "Actions speak louder than words" is a proverb.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Healthy Habits for Mind, Body and Soul

lessons.title: Healthy Habits for Mind, Body and Soul — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This article teaches the habits that empower people of any age to thrive. We get education for a better, more prosperous life, and good habits are the essential tools of a happy and fulfilling life — best learned in the teens, because habits developed now last a lifetime.

Habits for the Body

  • Keep a good schedule — our bodies perform best on a regular routine: eat and sleep at about the same time each day. Regular, uninterrupted sleep is essential; people who do not sleep soundly find it difficult to concentrate and complete their work.
  • Eat a healthy diet — the brain needs the right food to perform at its peak, so students should not go to school on an empty stomach. Teenagers need more nutritious food as their bodies change, but many start eating junk food loaded with sugar and harmful chemicals, and peer pressure leads some to over-eating or under-eating. Good nutrition is the key to a healthy life.
  • Learn to exercise — follow exercise routines and play sports and games that are fun, like volleyball, badminton or cricket.
  • Maintain good personal hygiene — washing hands, bathing regularly, brushing teeth twice a day, grooming hair and wearing a neat uniform keep us healthy and make the first impression impressive.

Habits for the Mind

  • Practice gratitude — do not fall into the bad habit of envying what others possess ("the grass often seems greener on the other side of the fence"). Be thankful for what you have and recall the good things happening every day.
  • Never give up — "Winners never quit and quitters never win." It takes perseverance to enjoy any success; give every task your best effort and strive for excellence in all you do.
  • Be a regular reader — "Good readers make good leaders." Reading builds vocabulary, expands the imagination and rekindles creativity.
  • Always tell the truth — the truth comes out sooner or later; lying only complicates the situation and makes us look bad.

Habits for Society and the Soul

  • Protect the environment — be mindful about plastic bags, littering and wasting natural resources: conserve water, use less paper, use biodegradable materials and plant more trees. Conservation protects our own survival.
  • Live the golden rule — "Do unto others what you expect others to do unto you": treat others well if you want to be treated well. Respecting diversity of race, belief and opinion, and avoiding conflict, is a hallmark of a successful life.
  • Respect traffic rules — never drive before 18: underage drivers are untrained, prone to road-rage and over-speeding, and teen drivers aged 14–19 are four times more likely to crash than older drivers.
  • Turn to your spiritual needs — take care of the soul to live a full and rewarding life; approach every situation with love and compassion, for "Allah loves those who do good" (Surah Ale Imran: 149).

Key Points

  • Eat nutritious food; avoid junk food and dieting fads driven by peer pressure.
  • Gratitude, perseverance and regular reading build the mind.
  • The golden rule, truthfulness, care for the environment and respect for traffic rules build a good life.

lessons.title: Unit 5 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 5 teaches the kinds of verbs and the difference between denotation and connotation.

Kinds of Verbs

  • Main (lexical) verbs show the main action or state of the subject. Action verbs show physical or mental action (run, write, think — She runs every morning); state verbs show a state or condition (know, believe, seem, love — He knows the answer).
  • Auxiliary (helping) verbs help the main verb form tenses, questions, negatives and voices. Primary auxiliaries: be, do, have (She is going; They have eaten). Modal auxiliaries: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must (You must study harder).
  • Transitive verbs require an object to complete their meaning: He kicked the ball. ("Ball" is the object of "kicked".)
  • Intransitive verbs need no object: She sleeps peacefully.
  • Linking verbs connect the subject to a subject complement (an adjective or noun): be, become, seem, appear, look, feel — She is tired. He became a doctor. The flower smells sweet.
  • Regular verbs form the past tense by adding -ed: walk → walked, play → played.
  • Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: go → went, eat → ate, write → wrote.

Denotation and Connotation

  • Denotation is the literal, dictionary definition of a word — its explicit, objective meaning, free of emotional association.
  • Connotation is the emotional, cultural or social association a word carries beyond its literal definition. Connotations can be positive, negative or neutral.
  • Home — denotation: a place where one lives, a residence. Connotation: warmth, comfort, safety and a sense of belonging.
  • Snake — denotation: a long, legless reptile that slithers and often has a venomous bite. Connotation: usually deceit or betrayal, though in some cultures snakes symbolize healing or transformation.

Key Points

  • A transitive verb takes an object; an intransitive verb does not.
  • Linking verbs join the subject to a complement: She is tired.
  • Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling attached to a word.

lessons.title: Nature — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Nature is a sonnet (a poem of fourteen lines) by the American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882). In it, Nature is personified as a fond mother, and death is presented not as a terror but as a gentle bedtime.

The Octave: The Mother and the Child

As a fond (loving) mother, when the day is over, leads her little child to bed by the hand — the child half willing, half reluctant (unwilling) to be led, leaving his broken playthings (toys) on the floor, still gazing at them through the open door, not wholly reassured and comforted by promises of other playthings in their stead (place), which, though more splendid, may not please him more — so does Nature deal with us.

The Sestet: Nature Leads Us to Rest

So Nature deals with us: she takes away our playthings one by one, and by the hand leads us to rest so gently that we go, scarce knowing if we wish to go or stay, being too full of sleep to understand how far the unknown transcends (goes beyond) what we know.

What the Symbols Mean

  • The child symbolizes humanity — every human being.
  • The playthings are the pleasures, possessions and attachments of earthly life, which are taken away one by one as we grow old.
  • Bedtime and sleep stand for death; the unknown world beyond is the room the child has not yet seen.
  • The fond mother is Nature herself — man's friend, philosopher and guide.

Theme

Man's life on earth is a long, toilsome journey that leads him to the world beyond through the gateway of death, and Nature constantly guides us on this journey and finally leads us to our destination. The poem's tone is calm: for a person who fears death, the message is comforting — death comes as gently as a mother leading a sleepy child to bed, and the unknown transcends (is far greater than) what we know. The central idea lies in the final six lines: Nature leads us gradually towards death, and we follow, half willing, half reluctant, like the child.

Key Points

  • "Nature" is a sonnet; Nature is personified as a fond mother.
  • The child = humanity; the playthings = earthly pleasures; bedtime = death.
  • The child is half willing, half reluctant — just as man clings to life yet must leave it.
  • The poem makes death gentle and peaceful, not fearful.

lessons.title: Unit 6 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 6 teaches phrases — prepositional, adjectival and adverbial — and the rhyme scheme of a poem.

Prepositional Phrase

A prepositional phrase is a group of words consisting of a preposition, its object, and any words that modify the object. Most of the time it modifies a verb or a noun: We are on the way to Peshawar. The cat is under the table. The keys are in the drawer. There are two kinds of prepositional phrases: adjectival and adverbial.

Adjective Phrase

An adjective phrase acts as an adjective by describing a noun.

  • A very tall building is under construction. ("Very tall" modifies "building".)
  • The man with the red hat is my uncle. ("With the red hat" modifies "man".)
  • He was wearing a crown made of gold.
  • The girl with the long hair is a talented singer.

Adverbial Phrase

An adverbial phrase acts as an adverb, modifying the verb, an adjective or another adverb, and tells how, when or where.

  • They will arrive in the morning. (when)
  • He works at a slow pace. (how)
  • He speaks with great enthusiasm.
  • She ran as fast as she could.

Rhyme Scheme

A rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhymes at the ends of the lines of a poem, shown with letters: lines that rhyme get the same letter. Rhyme scheme gives poetry structure and rhythm, making it melodious and memorable. In Wordsworth's "Daffodils", shine/line rhyme (A), way/bay rhyme (B), and glance/dance rhyme (C), so the scheme is ABABCC. In Kenn Nesbitt's "My Cat", nice/mice rhyme and around/sound rhyme, giving AABB.

Intonation (from the Oral Work)

Intonation is the rising or falling of the speaking voice. A rising pattern can show surprise or disbelief ("Really?"), a falling pattern shows confirmation or sarcasm ("Really."), and a rise-fall can show suspicion or hesitation. Intonation does not change the meaning of words, but it reflects the speaker's emotions and attitude.

Key Points

  • A prepositional phrase = preposition + object (+ modifiers).
  • An adjective phrase describes a noun; an adverbial phrase modifies a verb, adjective or adverb.
  • Rhyme scheme is written in letters, e.g. ABABCC.

lessons.title: Pakistan's Tourist Attractions — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This magazine article (adapted from Diplomat Magazine) presents Pakistan as a land of some of the most diverse natural beauty on the planet — a kaleidoscope of landscapes, a cradle of ancient civilizations and a melting pot of religions and cultures.

The World's View

  • Forbes ranked Pakistan among the "10 Coolest Places to go in 2019".
  • Condé Nast Traveller ranked Pakistan No. 1 on its list of 20 best holiday destinations for 2020.
  • Lonely Planet called Pakistan "tourism's next big thing".
  • The British Backpacker Society declared Pakistan the world's third best potential adventure destination for 2020, and earlier said Pakistan "tops the list of world's best travel destinations", calling it one of the friendliest countries on earth.
  • The World Economic Forum placed Pakistan among the top 25 per cent of global destinations for its UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Foreign tourist arrivals grew from less than half a million in 2015 to over two million in 2019, and domestic tourism crossed 40 million.

Mountains and the Highest Trade Route

Pakistan's ranges — the Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindukush — hold five of the world's fourteen highest peaks, the tallest being K2 (8,611 metres), the second highest peak in the world. The 806 km Karakoram Highway, built along the ancient Silk Road linking Pakistan to China, is the highest trade route in the world; over this road once travelled Marco Polo, the Chinese monk Fa Hien and Al-Beruni.

The Provinces

  • Punjab — rich agricultural lands, rivers, shrines, forts and gardens of the Mughal era; over 2,000 years ago the Gandhara Buddhist civilisation flourished here, with Taxila as the principal seat of Buddhist learning.
  • Balochistan — mountain ranges, mines and a very long coastal belt with the newly developed Gwadar Port; famous caves (Juniper Shaft Cave, Shahre-e-Roghan, Mangocher Cave), the ancient site of Mehrgarh, Hingol National Park, Kund Malir Beach, the juniper forests of Ziarat and the Moola Chotok waterfalls.
  • Sindh — home to the ancient city of Mohenjo-daro (Indus Valley Civilisation), the commercial hub Karachi, seaports and beaches on hundreds of miles of coastline.
  • Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — the scenic valleys of Swat and Kalam, skiing at Malam Jabba, the historic Khyber Pass and Peshawar, and the valleys of Naran and Kaghan.
  • Northern Areas — spread over 72,496 square km, the serene valleys of Gilgit, Hunza and Skardu lie amid snow-clad peaks several over 8,000 metres; Naltar in Gilgit-Baltistan hosted an International Skiing Cup in February 2019 with skiers from 13 countries.

Heritage and Religious Tourism

Pakistan is home to the Indus Valley Civilization (2,500–1,500 BC), one of the oldest in the world, and modern Pakistanis are a blend of Harappan, Indo-Aryan, Afghan, Arab, Turkic and Mughal heritages. Its vegetation and fauna range from alpine meadows and coniferous forests to the Indus plain, desert and coastline. For pilgrims, Pakistan preserves Buddhist relics and the ruins of Taxila, historic churches across the country, the Sikh heritage of Nankana Sahib (birthplace of Baba Guru Nanak) and the Kartarpur Corridor opened for visa-free Sikh pilgrimage, and the shrines of Sufi saints such as Data Ganj Bakhsh (Lahore), Abdullah Shah Ghazi (Karachi), Lal Shahbaz Qalandar (Sehwan Sharif) and Bahauddin Zakaria (Multan), who preached peace and universal love. The visit of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge gave Pakistan's tourism a further boost of confidence.

Key Points

  • Pakistan holds five of the world's fourteen highest peaks; K2 is 8,611 m, second highest in the world.
  • The Karakoram Highway is the highest trade route in the world.
  • Taxila was the seat of the Gandhara Buddhist civilisation; Mohenjo-daro belongs to the Indus Valley Civilization.
  • Religious tourism covers Buddhist, Christian, Sikh and Sufi sites, including the Kartarpur Corridor.

lessons.title: Unit 7 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 7 teaches the types of pronouns and the conventions of Standard English: capitalization, punctuation, spelling and hyphenation.

Pronouns and Their Types

A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun to avoid repetition: Ali is a student. He studies hard.

TypeFunctionExamples
PersonalRefer to specific people or thingsI, you, he, she, it, we, they, me, us — She is going to the market.
PossessiveShow ownership or possessionmine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs — This book is mine, not yours.
ReflexiveRefer back to the subject of the sentencemyself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves — He hurt himself while playing.
DemonstrativePoint to specific things or peoplethis, that, these, those — These are my favorite shoes.
InterrogativeUsed to ask questionswho, whom, whose, which, what — Who is knocking at the door?
RelativeLink a clause to a noun or pronounwho, whom, whose, which, that — The girl who won the prize is my cousin.
IndefiniteRefer to non-specific people or thingssomeone, anybody, everyone, few, many — Someone left his bag on the bench.
ReciprocalShow mutual action or relationshipeach other, one another — They helped each other during the project.

Conventions of Standard English

  • Capitalization — capital letters begin sentences and mark proper nouns, titles and important words in headings: We visited the National Museum of Pakistan.
  • Punctuation — periods, commas, question marks, quotation marks, apostrophes, colons and semicolons convey meaning clearly: After the rain stopped, we went outside to play.
  • Spelling — spell common and subject-specific words accurately; use dictionaries and proofreading.
  • Hyphenation — hyphens join words to form compound terms or prevent ambiguity: compound adjectives (a well-known author, a five-year-old child), prefixes (re-enter, co-operate), and word division at line breaks only when necessary. Note the difference: "my brother-in-law works in a well-known company" and "a two-day trip".
  • Present work legibly and neatly: clear handwriting, consistent margins and spacing, revised and proofread.

Key Points

  • There are eight types of pronouns, from personal to reciprocal.
  • Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject: He hurt himself.
  • Hyphens join compound adjectives before a noun: a well-known author.

chapters.title: Unit 8: The Power of Innovation, Creativity, and Success (Dialogue)

lessons.title: The Power of Innovation, Creativity, and Success — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This unit is a dialogue between two students, Ali and Hamza, sitting on a bench in the college garden after a career seminar on "Future Careers". Their talk answers one question: what does success mean in the 21st century?

Hard Work Is Not Enough

Ali used to think success came only through hard work and following a set path — study hard, get a job, work your way up. Hamza agrees that hard work is important, but says it is no longer enough on his own: "Hard work might get you in the game, but innovation and creativity are what make you stand out." His example is Elon Musk, the visionary whose companies Tesla and SpaceX succeeded because he imagined things differently and brought to life new ideas that others were afraid to try.

What Creativity and Innovation Mean

  • Creativity is the ability to think in new ways and to see connections others might miss. It does not belong only to artists or designers — it plays a big role in science, maths and business too. Using solar panels in rural areas where electricity is limited is creative problem-solving.
  • Innovation is creativity applied with a purpose: solving real problems in new ways. Ali's example is a student who designed a low-cost wheelchair using bicycle parts to help disabled people in villages — "innovation with a purpose", not fancy technology.
  • During the COVID-19 pandemic the whole world had to innovate: schools shifted to online classes, people started home businesses, and doctors treated patients by video calls. As the saying goes, "Necessity is the mother of invention."

Failure Is Part of the Journey

Thomas Edison tried more than a thousand times before inventing the light bulb; he did not call it failure — he called it learning. So failure is not the opposite of success; it is a part of it. The key is to keep learning and improving, and to have the courage to take risks. Schools should therefore develop creativity and innovation instead of only memorization — even writing stories or poems in English class builds creative thinking.

The Conclusion

Employers today look for people who can solve problems, produce new ideas and adapt to change. Success today is not only about studying or getting a degree; it is about using your mind in new ways, solving problems, and using your skills to help others — true success brings change in society. And the best part, says Hamza, is that everyone has the ability to be creative: we just have to practise, stay curious, and not be afraid to take risks.

Key Points

  • Hard work gets you in the game; innovation and creativity make you stand out.
  • Creativity = thinking in new ways; innovation = applying it to solve real problems.
  • Failure is part of success — Edison tried over a thousand times.
  • True success also means using your skills to help others.

Key Points

  • Innovation introduces new ideas; creativity produces original ideas.

  • To stand out is to be noticeably different in a good way.

lessons.title: Unit 8 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 8 teaches clauses, the types of adjectives, and how to construct complex sentences.

Clauses

A clause is a group of words that includes a subject and a verb, and forms a sentence or part of a sentence.

  • A main (independent) clause can stand alone and makes complete sense: Today is Wednesday. I was not keeping well, so I took a day off work.
  • A subordinate (dependent) clause has a subject and verb and begins with a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun; it cannot stand alone: After we reached home, we watched a movie. She stayed at home because it was raining.
  • Dependent clauses include noun clauses, adjective clauses, adverb clauses, conditional clauses, relative clauses, comparative clauses, verbless clauses and complementary clauses.
  • A relative clause modifies a noun or noun phrase and usually begins with a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) or a relative adverb (when, where, why): The boy who is wearing a blue cap is my cousin. This is the house where I was born. The only thing that matters is to find our way home.

Types of Adjectives

TypeFunctionExamples
DescriptiveDescribes the quality or characteristic of a nountall, beautiful, cold, soft — The tall man walked into the room.
QuantitativeShows the quantity or amountsome, few, many, several, all — We have many books in our library.
NumeralShows the exact number or orderone, two, first, second, tenth — He came second in the race.
DemonstrativePoints out specific nounsthis, that, these, those — These apples are fresh.
PossessiveShows ownership or possessionmy, your, his, her, their, our — Her bag is on the table.
InterrogativeUsed to ask questions about a nounwhich, what, whose — Which book do you like best?
DistributiveRefers to individual members of a groupeach, every, either, neither — Each student must bring their notebook.

Constructing Complex Sentences

A complex sentence joins a main clause to one or more subordinate clauses with a subordinating conjunction — sometimes called a "heart word", because it turns two sentences into one and makes one idea depend on the other. Common subordinating conjunctions: after, before, although, even though, as, because, if, since, so that, unless, until, when, whenever, where, whereas, while, whether.

  • Simple: He studied hard. He wanted to go to medical college. Complex: He studied hard because he wanted to go to medical college.
  • A dependent clause alone is wrong: "When he came late to class." Right: "He forgot to give the teacher his homework when he came late to class."
  • Comma rule: if the subordinating conjunction is in the middle or at the end, no comma is needed (School is not all about studying since there are lots of clubs). If the sentence begins with the dependent clause, put a comma at the end of that clause (Even though I would rather go to the beach, I went to the library to study).

Key Points

  • An independent clause stands alone; a dependent clause cannot.
  • Relative clauses begin with who, whom, whose, which, that, when, where or why.
  • A sentence beginning with a dependent clause needs a comma after that clause.

chapters.title: Unit 9: Youth and Age (Poem - S. T. Coleridge)

lessons.title: Youth and Age — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Youth and Age by Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834), a founder of the Romantic Movement in England, is a lament for lost youth — and, at the same time, a refusal to let youth go. The speaker looks back at what he was and measures it against what he has become.

Youth Remembered

In youth, verse, a breeze straying among blossoms, Hope clinging and feeding like a bee — all were his: "Life went a-maying with Nature, Hope, and Poesy, when I was young!" His body — "this breathing house not built with hands" — then flashed lightly along over aery cliffs and glittering sands, like trim skiffs (light boats) that ask no aid of sail or oar and fear no wind or tide. "Nought cared this body for wind or weather, when Youth and I lived in't together." Flowers are lovely; Love is flower-like; Friendship is a sheltering tree; and the joys of Friendship, Love and Liberty came down shower-like — before he was old.

The Change: 'Twixt Now and Then

"When I was young? — Ah, woful When! Ah! for the change 'twixt Now and Then!" The speaker cannot believe Youth is truly gone: Youth's vesper-bell (evening bell) has not yet tolled, and Youth was always a masker bold — a player in disguise — so perhaps this aged appearance is only another strange disguise. He sees his own locks in silvery slips, his drooping gait (tired manner of walking) and altered size, yet spring-tide blossoms are still on Youth's lips: "Life is but thought: so think I will that Youth and I are house-mates still."

Old Age Faced Honestly

The last stanza turns mournful: dew-drops are the gems of morning, but tears are the gems of mournful eve (evening of life). Where no hope is, life is only a warning that serves to make us grieve when we are old — like a poor relation who has outstayed his welcome and tells the jest without the smile.

Theme and Tone

The theme is the transience of life and the inevitability of aging: the lamentation of lost youth together with a steadfast grip on youthful hope despite physical aging. Youth is shown with images of blossoms, breezes, light skiffs and showering joys; age with silvery locks, drooping gait and tears. The tone shifts from nostalgic and sorrowful to quietly hopeful — the speaker accepts aging while keeping his inner youth alive: in thought, Youth and he are house-mates still.

Key Points

  • Youth = blossoms, breeze, light skiffs, shower-like joys; Age = silver locks, drooping gait, tears.
  • The speaker addresses Youth directly (apostrophe): "O Youth! for years so many and sweet."
  • "Life is but thought" — he resolves to believe Youth still lives with him.
  • Central theme: change — the passing of youth and the coming of age.

lessons.title: Unit 9 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 9 teaches adverbs, pronoun–antecedent agreement, and the twelve tense forms.

Adverbs and Their Types

An adverb adds information about place, time, manner, cause or degree to a verb, an adjective, a phrase or another adverb.

TypeTellsExamples
MannerHow an action is performedquickly, slowly, carefully, loudly — She quickly packed her bag.
TimeWhen an action happenstoday, soon, yesterday, now — He will come soon.
PlaceWhere an action happenshere, there, outside, upstairs — The kids are playing outside.
FrequencyHow often an action happensalways, never, often, sometimes — She often visits her grandmother.
DegreeIntensity or degreevery, quite, almost, too — It's very hot in the room.

Adverbs can stand at the front (Suddenly, the lights went out), in the middle (He always brings his lunch) or at the end (He reads quietly). When two or more adverbs follow a verb, the order is manner → place → time: Fahad performed brilliantly (how) at the Finance Conference (where) last Friday (when).

Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement

The antecedent is the word that comes before a pronoun and to which the pronoun refers; the pronoun must agree with it in number.

  • Singular indefinite pronouns take singular pronouns: Each of these gadgets has its own pros and cons.
  • Plural indefinite pronouns (several, few, both, many) take plural pronouns: Several applicants submitted their applications.
  • Two nouns joined by and take a plural pronoun: Laraib and Beena said they will go to the mall.
  • With or/nor: two singular nouns take a singular pronoun (Neither Ali nor Saleem was ready to lend me his book); a singular and a plural noun — the pronoun agrees with the nearest noun.
  • Collective nouns (committee, family, group, team) take a singular pronoun when the group acts as one unit: The committee submitted its report today.

The Twelve Tenses

TenseFormulaExample
Simple PresentSubject + base verb / s-esShe writes stories.

lessons.title: Old Tree — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Old Tree is a philosophical short story by Naseem Achakzai, a contemporary Pakistani writer whose reflective prose explores human values, nature, spirituality and resilience through symbolism and dialogue.

The Peaceful Forest and the Coming Disaster

In one of the living forests of the world, peace had ruled for centuries: every creature, from animals and birds down to the smallest insect and the tiny larva of a butterfly, had its food with pleasure. Suddenly a sense of disturbance spread: birds flew to their nests, deer and rabbits hid in their holes, the strong and respected eagle did not appear, and an anthill at the foot of the Old Tree stood deserted — the ants had already sensed the coming disaster. Silence enveloped the land; even in snow or bitter cold such stillness had never been felt. The time-respected Old Tree of Knowledge — now completely dried up, leafless, its colour changed from brown to white like a huge piece of dried bone, its roots weak in their grip — thought that fear is poison to life and must be converted into courage. Looking from east to west and south to north, it saw the sign: a strong flood was approaching, to cross the forest and fall into the river on the south-west.

The Dialogue: Old Tree and Flood

The first wave swept away dry leaves and branches. The Flood, smiling like a devil, mocked the old, dried tree: "Be a part of the obedience of the whole forest, otherwise you are just nothing in front of me!" The Old Tree answered with confidence: the Flood was born only a few hours ago out of rain, and would itself be drowned in the river and vanish into the great Ocean. "You will change my position and you will change my function, but you will never ever change my structure and you will never finish my quality." Life, the Tree explained, is not power or supremacy; life is continuity — a link between past and present that makes the future. The Tree recalled its own past: sown as a small seed that an ant could have swallowed, grown into a young and mighty tree that sheltered caravans of men, animals, insects and birds, and now old and dry, yet still useful — an anthill at its feet, insects protected in its roots.

The Fall — and the Victory

The Flood first attacked the anthill, but a soft layer of dust covered its mouth like a shield and the wave passed over without damage. Then the Flood gathered all its strength and struck the Old Tree, whose weak roots could not bear the attack: it crashed to the earth with a last terrible crack that echoed through the jungle. But the Flood could carry it only a few yards — the younger trees held it with their young trunks like powerful arms, with love and respect. The flood's force weakened, died away at the shore of the river, and vanished forever. Life returned to normal; a white dove — which used to sit on the Old Tree's dry branches — found the fallen tree in the middle of the forest and sat on its head, as if paying a rich tribute from all over the forest.

The Ship

Later a carpenter carried the fallen tree to his factory and cut it into large planks of valuable wood. A businessman bought them and made a ship. When the ship was launched, the ocean ordered its waves to bow their heads in respect to the wood of the Old Tree, which had undergone the experiences of centuries. The flood's own water, having reached the ocean through the rivers, had to bow too — and received on its head the strong beats of the ship's oars, which were also made of the Old Tree's wood. The Old Tree had won, exactly as it had foretold.

Theme

The central theme is the triumph of wisdom, endurance and moral strength over destructive and temporary forces. True power lies in knowledge, patience and continuity, not in aggression or pride. The Flood symbolizes destruction and arrogance; the Old Tree symbolizes wisdom, patience and society's memory; its transformation into a ship symbolizes rebirth — a fall that is really a victory.

Key Points

  • The forest creatures sense the flood first; the Old Tree turns fear into courage.
  • The Flood boasts of power and supremacy; the Tree answers with wisdom: life is continuity.
  • The Tree falls, but the young trees hold it and the flood vanishes into the river.
  • Made into a ship, the Tree is honoured by the ocean — its fall becomes a victory.

  • A tribute shows respect and admiration.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 10 teaches prepositions (types, compound prepositions and prepositional phrases), gerunds, infinitives and participles, and the aspect of time.

Types of Prepositions

A preposition connects a noun, noun phrase or pronoun to another word — a verb, another noun, or an adjective.

TypeCommon WordsExample
Timein, on, at, since, for, before, after, during, untilShe arrived at 7 p.m.
Place / Positionin, on, at, under, over, behind, beside, near, betweenThe book is on the table.
Direction / Movementto, into, onto, out of, off, across, throughHe walked into the room.
Cause / Reason / Purposebecause of, due to, owing to, for, fromThe match was canceled because of the rain.
Manner / Instrumentby, with, like, asHe wrote the letter with a pen.
AgentbyThe cake was baked by my mother.
Measure / Standardper, by, ofApples are sold by the dozen.

Compound Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases

Compound (phrasal) prepositions are formed by joining two or three words: because of, instead of, according to, in front of, due to, in spite of, on behalf of, in addition to, with regard to, by means of, out of. Examples: According to her principal she is a good student. She succeeded in spite of the difficulties. I submitted the application on behalf of my friend. A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition): in the garden, on the table, because of the rain. The girl in the second row has recently joined.

Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles

  • A gerund is a verb + -ing form that functions as a noun: Reading helps you learn. She enjoys dancing. Swimming is good exercise. Cooking is her favorite hobby.
  • An infinitive is to + base form of a verb; it can act as a noun (I like to read), an adjective (She has a story to tell) or an adverb (He came to help).
  • A participle is a verb form used as an adjective or in verb tenses. Present participle = verb + -ing (The crying baby woke up; the barking dog); past participle = verb + -ed or irregular form (The broken vase was expensive; the closed shop).

Aspect of Time

The aspect of time shows how actions are placed in time — past, present or future — and whether they are completed, continuing or repeated. Present time: She writes poems every day. They are studying for exams. Past time: He visited his grandmother yesterday. I was reading when you called. Future time: We will travel next week. She is going to start a new job.

Key Points

  • Prepositions of agent use by; prepositions of direction show movement.
  • A gerund works as a noun; an infinitive is to + verb; a participle works as an adjective.
  • Compound prepositions like in spite of and on behalf of act as one word.

lessons.title: A Handful of Clay — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
A Handful of Clay is a story by Henry Van Dyke (1852–1933), told from the point of view of the clay itself — an autobiography of a piece of clay.

The Clay's Great Dreams

There was a handful of clay on the bank of a river — only common clay, coarse and heavy, but with high thoughts of its own value and wonderful dreams of the great place it would fill in the world. Around it, the trees whispered of glory, the flowers rejoiced in their beauty, and the river hurried proudly to its mighty work. Waiting blindly in its bed, the clay comforted itself: "My time will come. I was not made to be hidden forever. Glory and beauty and honour are coming to me in due season."

The Trials: Cart, Trough, Wheel and Oven

One day a flat blade of iron lifted the clay into a cart and carried it over a rough and stony road — but it was not afraid: "This is necessary. The path to glory is always rugged." Then came far worse: it was mixed, beaten, stirred and trampled in a trough; whirled on the potter's wheel until it seemed it must fly into a thousand pieces, pressed and moulded as it revolved; and finally shut in an oven with fierce, penetrating fire. Through all, it held itself together in confidence: "Surely I am intended for something splendid — perhaps an ornament of a temple, or a precious vase for the table of a king."

The Disappointment: A Common Flower-Pot

The baking finished, the clay saw itself for the first time in a pool of water: not a temple ornament, but a common flower-pot — straight and stiff, red and ugly. It murmured against its unknown maker: "Why hast thou made me thus?" It passed many days in sullen discontent. Then it was filled with earth, and something rough, brown and dead-looking was thrust into the earth. The clay rebelled: "This is the worst of all — to be filled with dirt and rubbish. Surely I am a failure."

The Reward: A Royal Sceptre of Lilies

In the greenhouse, sunlight fell warm on the pot and water was sprinkled over it; day by day something began to stir within — a new hope. One day the clay was carried into a great church, amid glorious music and flowers. A neighbouring vessel explained: "You are carrying a royal sceptre of lilies. Their petals are white as snow, and the heart of them is like pure gold. The people look this way because the flower is the most wonderful in the world — and the root of it is in your heart." Then the clay was content, and silently thanked its maker: though an earthen vessel, it held so great a treasure.

Theme

Endurance and patience is the main idea. The clay sets an example of bearing the ups and downs of life with perseverance: hardship is the shaping process, and in the end patience bears fruit. The clay's idea of its purpose changes — from personal glory, to bitterness, to the discovery that a humble vessel can carry a royal treasure. The story teaches that purpose is found not in fame but in service, and that the Maker's hands shape us through trials we cannot yet understand.

Key Points

  • The clay dreams of glory; its trials are the cart, the trough, the wheel and the oven.
  • It is disappointed to find itself a common flower-pot and rebels at being filled with earth.
  • In the church it learns it carries a royal sceptre of lilies — and becomes content.
  • Lesson: endure with patience; a humble place can hold a great treasure.

  • To transform is to change form; to repent is to regret.
  • Obedient and rebellious are opposites; radiant means bright.

lessons.title: Unit 11 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 11 teaches modal verbs, the three kinds of conjunctions, and figurative language, word relationships and nuances.

Modal Verbs

Modal verbs are helping verbs used with main verbs to show ability, possibility, probability, permission or necessity.

ModalFunctionExample
canability, permission, possibilityShe can swim very fast. Can I use your phone?
couldpast ability, polite request, possibilityHe could sing well as a child. Could you help me, please?
maypermission (formal), possibilityMay I come in? It may rain today.
mightpossibility (less certain)They might be at the library.
mustobligation, strong necessity, logical deductionYou must wear a uniform. That must be his brother.
shallsuggestion, offer, formal futureShall we go for a walk? I shall return tomorrow.
shouldadvice, mild obligation, expectationYou should drink more water.
willfuture certainty, willingnessI will help you with your homework.
wouldpolite request, hypotheticalWould you like some tea? I would travel if I had money.
ought tomoral duty, adviceWe ought to respect our elders.
cannot / can'tprohibition, impossibilityYou cannot enter the lab without permission.
must not / mustn'tstrong prohibitionYou must not cheat in the exam.

Three Kinds of Conjunctions

  • Coordinating conjunctions join two independent clauses — remembered by FANBOYS: for (reason), and (addition), nor (negative alternative), but (contrast), or (choice), yet (unexpected result), so (result). She stayed home, for she was feeling sick. It was late, so we went home.
  • Subordinating conjunctions join an independent clause to a dependent clause: because, although, if, unless, until, when, while, since, before, after, once, even though, so that. He could not attend the meeting because he was sick. You can't go out until you finish your homework.
  • Correlative conjunctions are pairs that connect equal elements: either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or, no sooner…than, rather…than, the more…the more. She is not only intelligent but also hardworking. Both Ali and Ahmed are playing cricket.

Figurative Language, Word Relationships and Nuances

  • Euphemism: a mild, polite way to express something unpleasant — He passed away (instead of He died); the company is downsizing.
  • Oxymoron: opposite words combined for effect — deafening silence, bittersweet, silent applause.
  • Word relationships: synonyms (big–large), antonyms (hot–cold), associations (doctor–hospital, teacher–classroom).
  • Nuances: slight differences of tone between near-synonyms — childish (negative) vs childlike (positive, innocent); slim (healthy) vs skinny; firm vs rude; old vs vintage.

Key Points

  • Must shows obligation; must not shows prohibition; may asks formal permission.
  • FANBOYS = the seven coordinating conjunctions.
  • Correlative conjunctions always work in pairs.
  • A euphemism softens; an oxymoron joins opposites.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Trees In The Traffic Island (Poem)

lessons.title: Trees In The Traffic Island — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Trees In The Traffic Island is a poem by Sibghatullah Khan, a contemporary Pakistani poet known for sharp environmental and social commentary.

City Trees: An Obedient Line

The trees planted in the traffic island stand "in a straight obedient line, all green smoked pale grey." They are completely different from the wild, feisty fellas in the woods — the forest trees that grow mischievously like boys, moving in all directions, mocking manners, laughing through inflated lungs. The city trees, hardly breathing, "grow respectfully in cages like slaves." Afraid of the trimmer's huge shears, they lie low and never step beyond the kerb (the edge of the pavement).

Billboards of Civilization

The poet calls these trees "billboards of civilization" — dwarfs cut to an appropriate shape, "just meant to please": artificial beauty, not living nature. Earth breathes hard when trees fall; people talk of her growing heat and warnings of global warming, yet they watch a "jerry-built jungle" (a poorly built city) grow, with chains around trees and flowers "trained to entertain."

Theme and Tone

The theme is the contrast between nature's freedom and human-imposed control. Sibghatullah Khan critiques how urbanization has turned living trees into decorative symbols rather than living organisms: modern civilization enslaves nature, cutting it to size, limiting its growth and silencing its natural beauty, transforming forests into lifeless ornaments. The tone is critical — the poem asks us to notice what we have done to nature in the name of development, and to let trees live as trees, not as ornaments.

Key Points

  • City trees stand in an obedient line, pale grey with smoke; forest trees grow wild and free like boys.
  • "Cages like slaves" = confinement; "billboards of civilization" = artificial beauty.
  • The poem criticizes urbanization for enslaving and silencing nature.
  • Tone: critical; message: nature must be respected, not merely decorated.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the poem's key phrases.

Words and Meanings

Word / PhraseMeaning

billboards of civilizationTrees used as showpieces or advertisements of modern city life — artificial beauty.

trained to entertainTrees forced to serve as decoration for people's pleasure.

Key Points

  • Obedient = disciplined; feisty = lively; kerb = edge of the pavement.
  • "Grow respectfully in cages like slaves" suggests confinement, not freedom.
  • "Trained to entertain" means the trees are kept merely decorative.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 12 teaches interjections, sentence construction for different genres, essential vocabulary, and the writing skills of summary, paraphrase and research ethics.

Interjections

Interjections express sudden feelings and emotions. They usually stand at the beginning of a sentence and form exclamatory sentences: Hurray! We won the match. Ouch! That really hurt badly. Wow! That is a beautiful dress indeed. Oh! That was unexpected. Whoa! That guy is unbelievably huge. Others: Alas! (grief — Alas! The news of his passing is heartbreaking), Oops! (a small mistake — Oops! I dropped my phone again), Bravo! (praise — Bravo! What a clever idea), Hush! (silence — Hush! Please be quiet during the performance), Hey! (attention).

Sentence Construction for Genres

Use the right sentence form and complexity for the kind of writing:

GenreSentence StyleExample
Narrativeaction and sequenceShe opened the door and stepped into the dark room.
Descriptivesensory detailsThe golden sun set behind the quiet hills.
Expositoryfacts stated clearlyWater boils at 100°C under normal pressure.
Argumentativeopinion with reasonsEducation should be free because it promotes equality.

Sentences may be simple, compound or complex; varied structures make writing more effective, coherent and appropriate to purpose and audience.

Essential Vocabulary

Good vocabulary improves comprehension and expression. Learn new words through context clues, word mapping (synonyms, antonyms, examples), wide reading, dictionaries and thesauruses, flashcards and word journals. Use new words actively in writing, discussion groups and public speaking; review them regularly and set small weekly goals.

Summary, Paraphrase and Research Ethics

  • A summary gives the main points of a text briefly, in your own words, objectively.
  • A paraphrase restates a passage fully in your own words, keeping the meaning.
  • Research ethics: gather information from multiple authentic sources (books, academic articles, credible websites); check each source's credibility; take proper notes; cite all references and give credit to original authors; never copy text without credit — that is plagiarism, a violation of research ethics. A scholarly journal article is the most reliable source for academic research.

Key Points

  • Interjections show sudden emotion and take an exclamation mark.
  • Match sentence style to genre: narrative = action, descriptive = senses, expository = facts, argumentative = reasons.
  • Summary shortens; paraphrase restates fully — both in your own words.
  • Always cite sources; copying without credit is plagiarism.

lessons.title: The Last Leaf — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Last Leaf is a famous short story by O. Henry (1862–1910), the American master of the surprise ending, author of "The Gift of the Magi" and "The Ransom of Red Chief."

Greenwich Village and Mr. Pneumonia

In Greenwich Village, New York — a quarter of wild, twisting streets where artists find cheap rooms with good light — two young women painters, Sue (from Maine) and Johnsy (from California), share a studio at the top of a three-storey building. In winter a cold stranger enters the village: Pneumonia, who touches one person here and another there with his icy fingers. He touches Johnsy, and she lies in bed, barely moving, looking through the window at the blank wall of the next house, where an old ivy vine grows.

Counting the Leaves

The doctor gives Johnsy only a small chance: "She has a chance, if she wants to live. If people don't want to live, I can't do much for them." Johnsy has fixed her mind on a strange idea. She counts the ivy leaves backwards — twelve, eleven, ten… "When the last one falls, I must go, too. I've known that for three days." Only five leaves remain. Sue pleads, scolds and coaxes, but Johnsy will only wait to see the last leaf fall before night. Downstairs lives old Behrman, a painter past sixty who for forty years has talked of painting a great masterpiece but has never begun it; he poses as a model for others and drinks too much, yet believes it his duty to protect the two girls. Sue tells him of Johnsy's fancy; he shouts at the foolishness — and comes up to sit for her picture.

The Leaf That Would Not Fall

That night a cold rain falls with snow, and the wind beats wildly — yet in the morning one leaf still hangs against the wall, dark green near the branch, yellow at the edges. All day it stays. Johnsy watches it long, then calls Sue: "I've been a bad girl, Sue. Something has made that last leaf stay there to show me how bad I was. It is wrong to want to die." She asks for a mirror, sits up, eats — and hopes again to paint the Bay of Naples one day. The doctor now says her chances are good.

Behrman's Masterpiece

But the doctor must also see Behrman, ill with pneumonia; there is no hope. The next day Johnsy is safe — and Sue tells her the truth: Behrman died in hospital after two days. On that stormy night he had been found wet and cold as ice, with a lantern and his paints — green paint and yellow paint. "Look out the window, dear, at the last leaf on the wall. Didn't you wonder why it never moved when the wind was blowing? Oh, my dear, it is Behrman's great masterpiece — he painted it there the night that the last leaf fell."

Theme

The central theme is hope, self-sacrifice and the power of art. Emotional strength and hope can influence physical healing: believing the last leaf held on, Johnsy chooses life. Behrman's quiet act — painting the leaf in the storm and giving his life for it — shows the compassion and selflessness that friendship and purpose can inspire. The last leaf, a symbol of hope, becomes his true masterpiece.

Key Points

  • Johnsy ties her life to the falling ivy leaves; the doctor says the will to live is half the cure.
  • Behrman, the "failed" painter of forty years, paints a leaf on the wall during the stormy night.
  • The unfalling leaf restores Johnsy's hope; she recovers.
  • Behrman dies of pneumonia — his painted leaf is the masterpiece he always promised.
